post1.text:
Most leaders scaling past $50M think their biggest problem is strategy. It is not. It is the version of themselves they have not yet become.

A recent Entrepreneur piece pointed out something worth sitting with: half the year is gone, and most leaders are nowhere near the person their January goals required them to be. That gap is not a motivation problem. It is a leadership lag problem.

Here is what that means for companies in growth mode:

1. The skills that got you to $50M actively work against you past $100M. Delegation is not a soft skill at this stage. It is a survival mechanism.

2. Your culture is a direct reflection of your unexamined habits, not your stated values. If the company feels stuck, look up, not around.

3. Leaders who scale successfully treat their own development as a business-critical investment, not a nice-to-have.

The company will only grow as fast as the person leading it.

So here is the honest question: what has your business outgrown about you this year?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire caught our attention. Buffini and Company just brought on three senior executives specifically to support their next phase of scaling.

This is a move most mid-market leaders wait too long to make.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Companies between $50M and $200M often have a founding leadership team that is talented but stretched dangerously thin. Adding senior capacity before you feel ready is not overhead. It is infrastructure.

If you are scaling a coaching or services business, or any high-growth organization, the question is not whether you can afford senior leadership. It is whether you can afford another 18 months without it.

In "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," Katherine Slain opens with a chapter titled "Lead Like Lives Depend On It." The premise is direct: at this level of growth, your leadership is not a personal development topic. It is an organizational risk factor.

Katherine makes the case that scaling companies do not fail because of bad markets or poor products. They stall because the leader at the top has not made the hard internal changes that the next stage of growth demands.

There is a specific shift in mindset required. And most leaders miss it entirely until the damage is already done.

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit six months too late. By then, the multiple is already set.

Valuation is not something that happens to you at the closing table. It is something you build deliberately, years in advance. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce recently reinforced what we see consistently with clients: the businesses that command the highest multiples are the ones that treated their exit as an operating discipline, not a transaction event.

Here is what that looks like in practice for companies in the $50M to $500M range:

First, recurring revenue is worth more than lumpy revenue. Buyers pay a premium for predictability, full stop. Second, owner dependency destroys value. If the business cannot run without you for 90 days, acquirers will price that risk into the deal. Third, clean financials are not a baseline expectation. They are a competitive advantage in a due diligence process.

You cannot manufacture these things in a sprint before you sell. They have to be baked into how you run the company today.

So here is the question: if a sophisticated buyer evaluated your business this quarter, what would they find?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur makes a point that every scaling company founder needs to hear: if you are waiting until you are ready to sell to build your exit plan, you have already waited too long.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. The ones that suffer at the negotiating table are not the ones with bad businesses. They are the ones with great businesses that were never structured with transferability in mind.

Recurring revenue, management bench strength, customer concentration ratios, and clean cap tables are not things you fix in 90 days. They take years to engineer. And each one moves your multiple in a meaningful way.

If exit readiness is not on your leadership agenda today, it should be. Start the conversation now.

Exit planning gets treated like a finish line. Our new book argues it is actually a starting point.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman. They work in the M&A trenches and bring a perspective that most growth-stage leaders never get access to until it is too late.

One thing the chapter addresses directly: your multiple is not determined by your revenue. It is determined by how a buyer perceives the risk of owning your business after you leave. That distinction changes how you think about every operational decision you make between now and a transaction.

post1.text:
Most companies don't fail at strategy. They fail at the gap between deciding and doing.

A Forbes analysis on strategy execution found that leadership teams consistently collapse not from bad ideas, but from broken follow-through. The plan looks great in the boardroom. Ninety days later, nothing has moved.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They confuse activity with progress. Busy teams aren't executing teams. If you can't trace daily work back to a strategic priority, you don't have execution. You have motion.

2. Accountability is assigned but never designed. Ownership without a clear definition of done is just wishful thinking.

3. Strategy reviews happen too infrequently to course-correct. By the time leadership notices drift, months are gone.

For companies pushing past $50M, the bottleneck is almost never the strategy itself. It is the operating rhythm that was never built to carry it.

So here is the real question: does your team know, right now, what they are supposed to stop doing to make the strategy work?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams fall apart when it comes to strategy execution, and the findings are worth sitting with if you run a company between $50M and $500M.

The core issue is not capability. It is structure. Most leadership teams were built to manage, not to execute strategy at scale. Those are two different operating modes, and conflating them is expensive.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Companies at this stage have outgrown their original planning process but haven't replaced it with anything built for the complexity they are now operating inside.

If your leadership team leaves every quarterly planning meeting energized and then watches priorities quietly dissolve by week six, this article is worth your time.

post3.text:
The gap between strategy and execution is not a technology problem or a talent problem. It is a lessons-learned problem. And sometimes the best lessons come from selling fish food and Nike shoes.

Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," is written by Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall. They bring something most strategic planning chapters don't: real pattern recognition from industries that look nothing alike on the surface but share the same execution breakdowns underneath.

One of the sharpest insights in this chapter is that scaling companies rarely fail because the strategy was wrong. They fail because the people responsible for executing it were never given a clear line of sight from their daily decisions to the company's direction.

That distinction changes how you build your planning process entirely.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked three years ago. A strategy is a deliberate system built around how your ideal buyers actually make decisions today.

Gartner recently found that AI is saving sales teams real time, but that time savings is not converting to revenue growth unless sales leadership actively redesigns how the team works. That gap is not a technology problem. It is a strategy problem.

Here is what that means for scaling companies:

1. Efficiency without direction is just faster mediocrity. Time saved is worthless if reps fill it with low-value activity.

2. Buyer behavior has shifted faster than most sales processes. If your playbook is more than 18 months old, it is probably misaligned.

3. Revenue growth at this stage is a leadership decision, not a hiring decision. More reps running a broken strategy just scales the loss.

What does your sales strategy actually tell your team to stop doing?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Gartner makes a point that every Chief Sales Officer at a scaling company needs to read: AI is saving sales reps time, but that time is not translating into revenue unless sales leadership steps in and redirects it.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. They invest in tools, add headcount, and wonder why the top line is not moving proportionally. The answer is almost always the same. There is no real sales strategy underneath the activity.

AI can optimize execution. It cannot create direction. That is a leadership job.

If you are scaling a business and your sales results feel random, start by asking whether your team is executing a strategy or just staying busy.

Read the Gartner piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg

post3.text:

Chapter 4 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled 'Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation.' It was written by Deb and Brandon, and the core argument is one that most $50M companies are not ready to hear.

The absence of a defined sales strategy is not neutral. It costs you money every single day. Not because your team is lazy, but because effort without architecture does not compound.

Deb and Brandon lay out what a real sales strategy looks like at this stage of growth, and why the tactics most teams rely on are actually holding them back from the next level.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M+ are still treating marketing like a megaphone. Louder. More campaigns. More channels. That is not strategy. That is noise with a budget.

JBL recently shifted their entire marketing approach away from discrete campaigns and toward building something inside culture itself. The result is a brand that does not need to interrupt people because people are already part of it.

Here is what that means for scaling companies:

1. Your brand is not your logo or your tagline. It is the feeling people carry after every interaction with your company, including the ones your marketing team never touches.

2. At $50M, you can still rely on founder reputation. At $150M+, you need a brand that operates independently of any single person.

3. Consistency compounds. A brand that smells the same across every channel, every quarter, every hire builds trust faster than any campaign ever could.

So here is the real question: If your company went silent for 90 days, would your brand still be recognizable in the market?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Brand Innovators caught our attention. JBL is walking away from the traditional campaign model and building its marketing around culture instead.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is not just a creative decision. It is a structural one.

Campaigns have an end date. Culture does not. When your marketing is rooted in something your customers already believe in or aspire to, you stop renting attention and start earning it.

The companies we work with that scale fastest are the ones who figure out what their brand actually stands for before they scale their marketing spend. More dollars behind a blurry brand just creates expensive confusion.

Read the full piece and ask yourself whether your marketing is building something lasting or just filling a quarter.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost strategy.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to headcount as the answer to every operational problem. More revenue means more people. More problems mean more people. The math feels obvious until your margins collapse and your culture fractures under the weight of people who were never the right fit to begin with.

SHRM's recent research on 2026 hiring trends confirms what the best operators already know: precision beats scale every time. The companies winning the talent game are not the ones posting the most jobs. They are the ones getting ruthlessly specific about what a role actually needs to produce, who can realistically produce it, and what it will cost the business to get it wrong.

Three things scaling companies get wrong on talent:

1. They hire for immediate pain relief instead of future capability.
2. They confuse culture fit with skill fit.
3. They treat onboarding as an HR task instead of a revenue function.

The question is not how fast you can fill a seat. It is whether the person in that seat will still be the right hire 18 months from now. Are you hiring for today or building for tomorrow?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business Wire announced that Ouster named Shaluinn Fullove as their new Chief People Officer, specifically to lead global growth and talent strategy.

Notice the framing: not HR. Not workforce management. Talent strategy tied directly to growth.

That distinction matters enormously for companies scaling from $50M toward $500M. At that stage, people decisions are not administrative functions. They are the engine. Who owns talent at your company, and are they sitting in growth conversations or compliance conversations?

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams where talent accountability is still buried three layers below the CEO. If your people strategy does not have an executive owner with real authority and a seat at the revenue table, you are not scaling. You are gambling.

Read the full announcement here: https://news.google.

post3.text:
SHRM's research on precision hiring in 2026 is pointing at something our contributors have been watching for years in scaling companies.

Chapter 6 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond, is called The Talent Engine. Authors Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West lay out why most mid-market companies are not under-hiring. They are mis-hiring, and doing it at speed.

One idea that will stay with you: the cost of a wrong hire at the $50M to $500M stage is not just financial. It compounds into culture, retention, and the leadership pipeline you will desperately need 24 months from now.

The framework they share for getting this right is worth the read on its own.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at $50M+ companies are drowning in dashboards. Every department tracks something. Almost nobody agrees on what actually matters. The result is a lot of reporting and very little accountability.

Oracle NetSuite recently outlined the hospitality industry's most critical metrics, and what stood out was the discipline of the list. Eleven. Not forty-seven.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

First, they confuse activity metrics with outcome metrics. Tracking calls made is not the same as tracking revenue generated per rep.

Second, they let every department own its own scorecard. Without a unified view, the executive team is always translating instead of deciding.

Third, they review KPIs monthly when the business moves weekly. By the time the data is discussed, the opportunity to act has already passed.

The companies that scale well are ruthless about fewer, sharper numbers reviewed on the right cadence.

What would you cut if your leadership team could only track five metrics?

#BusinessScaling #ExecutiveLeadership #PerformanceManagement

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounded up 14 tools for tracking KPIs across your business. Useful list. But here is the thing most scaling companies miss: the tool is never the problem.

When a company is pushing past $50M, the KPI conversation is rarely about software. It is about alignment. Which metrics does the CEO see? Which ones does the frontline manager see? Do those two sets of numbers tell the same story?

Autobahn works with leadership teams every week who have invested in world-class dashboards and still cannot answer the question: are we winning?

Before you evaluate another platform, get clear on what your company's three to five non-negotiable numbers are. Then find a tool that surfaces those cleanly.

The article is worth a read as a starting point: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
Every growing company eventually hits the same wall. The metrics that helped you reach $50M start working against you on the way to $500M.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business, titled Death by KPIs, tackles this directly. Authors Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall have sat inside enough scaling companies to know that the danger is rarely too few metrics. It is almost always too many, tracked too loosely, by teams that are not sure who owns the outcome.

One insight the chapter surfaces: there is a meaningful difference between a metric that tells you what happened and a metric that tells you what to do next. Most leadership teams are heavy on the first and starving for the second.

If your weekly leadership meeting feels like a reporting session instead of a decision session, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

For companies scaling past $50M, bloated KPI stacks create the illusion of oversight while slowing down every real decision. The leaders who scale fastest are not the ones with the best dashboards. post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong. They treat it like a faster search engine instead of a force multiplier for leadership capacity.

The New York Times recently covered executives deploying AI twins to handle routine interactions and free up cognitive bandwidth. That is not a gimmick. That is a signal.

Here is what leaders at $50M and above should be thinking about right now:

1. AI does not replace your judgment. It removes the noise that crowds out your judgment. The executives winning with AI are protecting their highest-value thinking, not automating it away.

2. The productivity gap between AI-fluent leadership teams and everyone else is widening fast. This is becoming a competitive moat, not a nice-to-have.

3. Implementation is the actual problem. Most companies have access to the same tools. The ones scaling fastest have built internal habits and processes around those tools.

The question is not whether AI belongs in your business. The question is whether your leadership team is disciplined enough to use it strategically.

What is one decision you made last week that AI could have informed faster?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bloomberg surveyed twelve CEOs and executives on how they are actually using AI to save time and get more done. The answers were practical, specific, and honestly a little eye-opening.

What stood out to us at Autobahn: the leaders getting real results are not experimenting broadly. They are identifying one or two high-friction areas in their week and targeting those with precision.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, that focus matters even more. You do not have the slack of a Fortune 500 to absorb unfocused AI adoption. Every tool you bring in needs to earn its place in your operating rhythm.

If you are a senior leader trying to figure out where AI actually fits in your growth strategy, this article is a solid starting point.

Read it here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxNc010ZUhURC0wVGNKMTdRUWVyTnZFVXRWODBxaVc3MWYyeU52bG1PdHVaTU45aS1mSG13Ulh2eUtmcU5qNXhma2VDLWo0UlpDLWMyU0lZc1ZkcHZzZXVrVXlpNGNObGVxRnVTMlVBc2RQLTk2bWtJaWFmeW1BMlBHNml5SktYdEdaLWJ3VmpYTU55bHB6cVpUVW5LWG1WR2lhRng0SXYwcHdFYXJTanJn?oc=5

post3.text:
Executives using AI twins to reclaim their time. CEOs building AI habits into their daily operating systems. This is not a future trend. It is happening right now in the companies pulling ahead.

Chapter 8 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business tackles exactly this shift. Called The Third Monitor Theory, the chapter was co-authored by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it reframes how growth-stage leaders should think about AI, not as a department initiative, but as a personal leadership discipline.

The insight that will stick with you: the leaders who scale from $50M to $500M are not the ones with the best AI tools. They are the ones who have built the clearest boundaries around how and when those tools serve their decision-making.

There is a meaningful difference between AI that supports your thinking and AI that substitutes for it. That distinction is where most companies get it wrong.

The leaders most likely to derail your company's growth are not the incompetent ones. They are the ones who secretly believe they do not belong in the room.

Imposter syndrome does not disappear when you hit $50M in revenue. Research covered by Forbes confirms it follows high achievers straight to the top, often intensifying as the stakes grow larger.

Here is what that costs scaling companies specifically:

1. Leaders avoid bold decisions because being wrong feels like exposure, not a learning opportunity.

2. High-performing executives hesitate to hire people who are sharper than they are, which caps the team's ceiling.

3. Companies plateau not from lack of strategy but from the quiet self-doubt of the person executing it.

The fix is not a confidence seminar. It is building a leadership culture where internal doubt is named, normalized, and worked through as a business issue, not a personal weakness.

What is your organization actually doing to address the psychology of the people running it?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Seattle University outlines six practical ways leaders can work through imposter syndrome when stepping into a new leadership role. It is solid, actionable advice.

But here is what it does not address: at the $50M to $500M growth stage, leadership roles do not just change titles. They change identities. The skills that got your executives to this level are often not the ones that will carry the company forward, and that gap is fertile ground for imposter syndrome to take root and slow everything down.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders navigating exactly this transition. The companies that scale successfully treat the psychology of leadership as seriously as the strategy of growth.

How could you be wildly successful and still not feel like you earned it? That is not a rhetorical question. It is the title of Chapter 9 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

Chapter 9 was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, and it goes somewhere most business books refuse to go: the interior life of the leader driving growth.

One thing they surface that we think will hit close to home for a lot of executives: imposter syndrome at this stage of growth is not about self-esteem. It is about identity, and if you do not address it directly, it shapes your decisions in ways you cannot see from the inside.

post1.text:
The most dangerous moment in a founder's career is not a bad quarter. It is the moment after a major win.

Research from Entrepreneur confirms what we see repeatedly with scaling leaders: three out of four founders who exit their business report significant regret within the first year. Not because the deal was wrong. Because they never designed what came next.

Here is what leaders at the $50M to $500M stage need to hear:

1. Your business is not your identity, but if you have never separated the two, you will not know that until the business is gone.

2. Life planning is not retirement planning. It is deciding now what a great life looks like while you still have full leverage to build it.

3. The executives who scale best are the ones who bring the same rigor to designing their personal life that they bring to designing their org chart.

Most leadership teams spend hundreds of hours on strategic planning and zero hours on this.

So here is the question: when did you last put your own life on the whiteboard?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced with Morgan Stanley, laid out a roadmap for entrepreneurs navigating life after selling their business. It covers the financial side thoughtfully. But it largely skips the harder conversation: what do you actually do with yourself on Monday morning?

At Autobahn, we work with leaders scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The ones who struggle most after a liquidity event are not the ones who made a bad deal. They are the ones who never built a life outside the business.

The time to design that life is before the exit, not after.

If you lead a scaling company, this article is worth your 10 minutes. Then ask your leadership team: are we building a business that serves our lives, or replacing them?

Three out of four founders regret selling their business within a year. That statistic should stop every scaling leader cold.

Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled Coming Up for Air. Co-authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, this chapter tackles something most business books treat as an afterthought: how do you design a life that actually works while you are building a company worth having?

One of the core ideas in this chapter is that life planning is not something you do at the finish line. Leaders who wait until the exit to figure out who they are outside the business almost always pay for it.

The framework Samantha and the Slains share gives you a way to make those decisions with the same intentionality you bring to your growth strategy.
